claim: Ramón y Cajal proclaimed the neuron doctrine based on circuit features he exemplified using cerebellar basket cell projections.
source: Ramón y Cajal proclaimed the neuron doctrine based on circuit features he exemplified using cerebellar basket cell projections.
evidence: This is a historical statement supported by citation to established scientific knowledge about Cajal's work.

claim: Basket cells form dense inhibitory plexuses that wrap Purkinje cell somata and terminate as pinceaux at the initial segment of axons.
source: Basket cells form dense inhibitory plexuses that wrap Purkinje cell somata and terminate as pinceaux at the initial segment of axons.
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical description supported by the literature and confirmed by observations in this study.

claim: HCN1, Kv1.1, PSD95 and GAD67 mark patterns of basket cell pinceaux that map onto Purkinje cell functional zones.
source: Here, we demonstrate that HCN1, Kv1.1, PSD95 and GAD67 unexpectedly mark patterns of basket cell pinceaux that map onto Purkinje cell functional zones.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figures 1-5 showing zonal patterns of these markers.

claim: Basket cell zones comprise different sizes of pinceaux.
source: Using cell-specific genetic tracing with an Ascl1CreERT2 mouse conditional allele, we reveal that basket cell zones comprise different sizes of pinceaux.
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic labeling experiments shown in Figure 6 with quantitative analysis.

claim: Genetically silencing Purkinje cell neurotransmission blocks the formation of sharp Purkinje cell zones.
source: Genetically silencing Purkinje cell neurotransmission blocks the formation of sharp Purkinje cell zones and disrupts excitatory axon patterning.
evidence: This is supported by data from Pcp2Cre;Slc32a1flox/flox mice shown in Figure 7 and cited from White et al., 2014.

claim: The distribution of pinceaux into size-specific zones is eliminated without Purkinje cell GABAergic output.
source: The distribution of pinceaux into size-specific zones is eliminated without Purkinje cell GABAergic output.
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis in Figure 7 showing loss of pinceau size differences in Pcp2Cre;Slc32a1flox/flox mutants.

claim: Cajal's discovery that basket cell endings terminate upon the initial segment of Purkinje cells sparked a new era of neuroscience.
source: In particular, it was Cajal's discovery that the endings of basket cells terminate upon what would become known as the initial segment of Purkinje cells that sparked a new era of neuroscience (Cajal, 1911).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citation to Cajal's original work.

claim: The pinceau was named for its paintbrush-like appearance.
source: He called this nerve ending 'the pinceau', named for its paintbrush-like appearance.
evidence: This is a historical fact about the naming of the structure.

claim: Sanford Palay and Victoria Chan-Palay resolved the full architecture of basket cell axons using electron microscopy.
source: The complexity of the basket cell pinceau hid its true connectivity when studied using the Golgi reaction, although using electron microscopy, Sanford Palay and Victoria Chan-Palay resolved the full architecture of the basket cell axons, their collaterals, the pericellular baskets that wrap around the Purkinje cell soma, and the pinceau terminals that contact the initial segment of the Purkinje cell axon (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974).
evidence: This is a historical claim supported by citation to Palay and Chan-Palay's work.

claim: There is surprising sparseness of synaptic contacts between the pinceau and the Purkinje cell axon.
source: The surprising sparseness of synaptic contacts between the pinceau and the Purkinje cell axon (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974; Somogyi and Hámori, 1976)
evidence: This is supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: Advanced slice electrophysiology recording methods revealed an ultra-fast ephaptic mode of axon-to-axon communication between basket cells and Purkinje cells.
source: More than three decades later, advanced slice electrophysiology recording methods revealed an unexpected ultra-fast ephaptic mode of axon-to-axon communication between basket cells and Purkinje cells (Blot and Barbour, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blot and Barbour's electrophysiology study.

claim: Genetic silencing of GABAergic basket cell output alters Purkinje cell firing in vivo.
source: Accordingly, the collective repertoire of contacts between the two cell types makes a substantial functional contribution, as genetic silencing of GABAergic basket cell output alters Purkinje cell firing in vivo (Brown et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2019.

claim: Basket cells play an essential role in controlling cerebellar cortical output during motor behavior.
source: There is also evidence showing that basket cells play an essential role in controlling cerebellar cortical output during motor behavior (Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2008; Wulff et al., 2009; Jelitai et al., 2016; Gaffield and Christie, 2017; He et al., 2015; Sergaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Basket cells project in the sagittal plane.
source: Interestingly, basket cells project in the sagittal plane (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974)
evidence: This is supported by citation to anatomical studies.

claim: Purkinje cell molecular and functional heterogeneity are restricted to sagittal domains.
source: which is intriguing because Purkinje cell molecular and functional heterogeneity are restricted to sagittal domains (Apps et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Apps et al., 2018.

claim: Basket cells are coupled in sagittal rows.
source: especially since the basket cells are coupled in sagittal rows (Sotelo, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sotelo, 2015.

claim: The electrical and chemical connectivity coefficients of basket cells are strongly represented in the sagittal plane.
source: The electrical and chemical connectivity coefficients of basket cells are strongly represented in the sagittal plane (Rieubland et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rieubland et al., 2014.

claim: Cerebellar circuit maps are comprised of hundreds, perhaps thousands, of modules.
source: Cerebellar circuit maps are comprised of hundreds, perhaps thousands, of modules (Apps et al., 2018; Miterko et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent reviews.

claim: Each cerebellar module is assembled from an array of cell types that are arranged around Purkinje cell patterns.
source: Each module is assembled from an array of cell types that are arranged around Purkinje cell patterns (Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Apps and Hawkes, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews on cerebellar organization.

claim: Excitatory granule cells and unipolar brush cells are patterned in the cerebellum.
source: The surrounding cells are all patterned and include excitatory granule cells and unipolar brush cells (Sillitoe et al., 2003; Chung et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing patterning of these cell types.

claim: Inhibitory Golgi cells are patterned in the cerebellum.
source: inhibitory Golgi cells (Sillitoe et al., 2008a)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study showing Golgi cell patterning.

claim: Bergmann glia are patterned in the cerebellum.
source: and even Bergmann glia (Reeber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study showing Bergmann glia patterning.

claim: Excitatory climbing fiber afferents terminate in domains that respect Purkinje cell zones.
source: Excitatory climbing fiber and mossy fiber afferents also terminate in domains that respect Purkinje cell zones (climbing fibers–Gravel et al., 1987; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007b; Reeber and Sillitoe, 2011
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical tracing studies.

claim: Mossy fiber afferents terminate in domains that respect Purkinje cell zones.
source: mossy fibers–Brochu et al., 1990; Quy et al., 2011; Gebre et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical tracing studies.

claim: Basket cell pinceaux have different sizes, and their sizes are determined cell non-autonomously by Purkinje cell GABAergic neurotransmission.
source: We reveal that basket cell pinceaux have different sizes, and their sizes are determined cell non-autonomously by Purkinje cell GABAergic neurotransmission.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by genetic manipulation experiments in Figures 6-8.

claim: The cerebellar nuclei mediate the motor and non-motor functions of the cerebellum using ascending and descending projections to the thalamus, red nucleus, and inferior olive.
source: The cerebellar nuclei mediate the motor and non-motor functions of the cerebellum using ascending and descending projections to the thalamus, red nucleus, and inferior olive (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy and function, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The cerebellar cortex has three distinct layers.
source: The cerebellar cortex has three distinct layers (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The most superficial layer of the cerebellar cortex contains inhibitory interneurons called basket cells and stellate cells, as well as excitatory climbing fibers and parallel fibers.
source: The most superficial layer contains inhibitory interneurons called basket cells and stellate cells, as well as excitatory climbing fibers and parallel fibers (the axons of granule cells).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about cerebellar cortical organization.

claim: The Purkinje cell layer (PCL) is the middle cerebellar cortical layer.
source: All four cell types project onto the Purkinje cells, which make up the middle cerebellar cortical layer called the Purkinje cell layer (PCL).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The PCL contains candelabrum cells and large astrocytes called Bergmann glia.
source: The PCL also contains candelabrum cells and large astrocytes called Bergmann glia.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Purkinje cells perform the main computations in the cerebellum.
source: Purkinje cells perform the main computations in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar function.

claim: The granular layer (GL) is the deepest layer of the cerebellar cortex.
source: The deepest layer is called the granular layer (GL)
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The granular layer contains millions of excitatory neurons called granule cells.
source: and contains millions of excitatory neurons called granule cells
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The granular layer contains a smaller population of excitatory neurons called unipolar brush cells.
source: a smaller population of excitatory neurons called unipolar brush cells
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The granular layer contains inhibitory Lugaro cells.
source: inhibitory Lugaro cells
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Mossy fibers deliver sensory signals to the cerebellum from dozens of brain and spinal cord nuclei.
source: and input fibers called mossy fibers that deliver sensory signals to the cerebellum from dozens of brain and spinal cord nuclei (Figure 1A; White and Sillitoe, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HCN1 is a membrane protein that contributes to native pacemaker currents in the heart and nervous system.
source: HCN1, or hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated potassium channel 1, is a membrane protein that contributes to native pacemaker currents in the heart and nervous system (Chang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HCN1 function supported by citation.

claim: The four HCN channels are encoded by the HCN1-4 genes.
source: The four HCN channels are encoded by the HCN1-4 genes
evidence: This is established molecular biology knowledge.

claim: HCN channels modulate cellular excitability, rhythmic activity, dendritic integration, and synaptic transmission.
source: and together they modulate cellular excitability, rhythmic activity, dendritic integration, and synaptic transmission (Moosmang et al., 1999; Moosmang et al., 2001; Notomi and Shigemoto, 2004; He et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the cerebellum, HCN1 is expressed in Purkinje cells, where it mediates a large hyperpolarization-activated current (Ih).
source: In the cerebellum, HCN1 is expressed in Purkinje cells, where it mediates a large hyperpolarization-activated current (Ih) (Nolan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HCN1 is heavily expressed presynaptically in basket cell terminals.
source: However, it is also heavily expressed presynaptically in basket cell terminals (Santoro et al., 1997; Luján et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HCN1 shows a non-uniform pattern of expression on tissue sections cut through the adult mouse cerebellum.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that HCN1 shows a non-uniform pattern of expression on tissue sections cut through the adult mouse cerebellum (two different areas of cerebellar cortex are shown in Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a novel observation from this study shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ZebrinII is a polypeptide antigen found on the aldolase C protein.
source: ZebrinII is a polypeptide antigen found on the aldolase C protein (Ahn et al., 1994; Brochu et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Lobules I-V and anterior VIII-IX are identified by a striking array of zebrinII zones.
source: Lobules I-V and anterior VIII-IX are identified by a striking array of zebrinII zones, where lobules VI-VII and posterior IX-X express it uniformly (Sillitoe and Hawkes, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about zebrinII expression patterns supported by citation.

claim: The pattern of HCN1 respected the pattern of zebrinII, with an inverse relationship between the two.
source: We found that the pattern of HCN1 indeed respected the pattern of zebrinII, with an inverse relationship between the two.
evidence: This is a finding from the study demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: HCN1 expression was more prominent around Purkinje cells that did not express zebrinII.
source: HCN1 expression was more prominent around Purkinje cells that did not express zebrinII (Figure 2C–F)
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: There is a significant difference in the size of pinceaux between zebrinII-positive and zebrinII-negative zones.
source: We quantified pinceau expression in the P1+ to P3+ zones (and intervening P- zones) of lobule VIII (Figure 2H) and found a significant difference in the size of pinceaux between zebrinII-positive and zebrinII-negative zones (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study shown in Figure 2I.

claim: There is no difference in HCN1 intensity between pinceaux of different sizes.
source: We then tested whether this size difference was driven by an unequal intensity of protein expression. We found no difference in HCN1 intensity between pinceaux of different sizes (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study shown in Figure 2J.

claim: ZebrinII-positive zones are populated with basket cells with small pinceaux, while zebrinII-negative zones are populated with basket cells with large pinceaux.
source: Overall, these data suggested that zebrinII-positive zones were populated with basket cells with small pinceaux, while zebrinII-negative zones were populated with basket cells with large pinceaux (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Larger HCN1-expressing basket cell profiles localized around PLCβ4-expressing/zebrinII non-expressing Purkinje cells.
source: We therefore co-stained coronal-cut tissue sections with HCN1 and PLCβ4 (Figure 3A–F) and found that indeed, larger HCN1-expressing basket cell profiles localized around PLCβ4-expressing/zebrinII non-expressing Purkinje cells (P- zones in Figure 3G–H).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 3.

claim: Zones with high NFH expression correspond to distinct HCN1 zones in lobule VII.
source: After co-staining with HCN1 and NFH, we found that zones with high NFH expression correspond to distinct HCN1 zones in lobule VII (Figure 4A–C)
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: The relationship between NFH and HCN1 zones is maintained through lobules VIII and IX.
source: and maintain that relationship through lobules VIII (Figure 4D–F) and IX (Figure 4G–I).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 4D-I.

claim: The size difference between pinceaux in different zones was less apparent in lobule IX compared to that in VII or VIII.
source: We also observed that the size difference was less apparent in lobule IX compared to that in VII or VIII.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: The pinceau region was larger in NFH-positive zones compared to the negative zones.
source: We found that the pinceau region revealed by both of these markers was larger in NFH-positive zones compared to the negative zones.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study shown in Figure 4K.

claim: There was no overlap of pinceau size between positive and negative zones among any of the lobules included in the analysis.
source: Additionally, there was no overlap of pinceau size between positive and negative zones among any of the lobules included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: Kv1.1, PSD95, and GAD67 all adhere to the zonal boundaries.
source: Similar to HCN1, we found that Kv1.1, PSD95, and GAD67 all adhere to the zonal boundaries, as assessed on coronal-cut tissue sections from lobule VIII (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 5.

claim: All four basket cell markers (HCN1, Kv1.1, PSD95, GAD67) delineated the same spatial expression pattern, in the same zones.
source: Interestingly, all four markers revealed an identical staining pattern; that is, all four basket cell markers delineated the same spatial expression pattern, in the same zones.
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 5.

claim: An Ascl1CreERT2 allele can be used to mark and track basket cells based on their birth date during late embryogenesis.
source: We recently showed that an Ascl1CreERT2 allele can be used to mark and track basket cells based on their birth date during late embryogenesis (Brown et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2019.

claim: Oral gavage of tamoxifen to pregnant dams when their embryos are embryonic day (E) 18.5 labels a rich population basket cells with recombination at ~46% across the entire cerebellum.
source: We chose this genetic marking strategy because oral gavage of tamoxifen to pregnant dams when their embryos are embryonic day (E) 18.5 labels a rich population basket cells with recombination at ~46% across the entire cerebellum (Brown et al., 2019; the genetic strategy is schematized in Figure 6E)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2019 and illustrated in Figure 6E.

claim: The genetically marked basket cell pinceaux delineate a sharp boundary within the PCL.
source: The IP3R1 receptor uniformly marks Purkinje cells (Figure 6A), whereas the genetically marked basket cell pinceaux delineate a sharp boundary within the PCL (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The division of basket cell projections respects the boundaries of the Purkinje cell zones.
source: Labeling with PLCβ4 demonstrates that the division of basket cell projections respects the boundaries of the Purkinje cell zones (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The basket cell-to-Purkinje cell topography is not perfect at the zonal boundaries.
source: However, compared to the strict and uncompromising relationship between climbing fibers and Purkinje cells (Gravel et al., 1987; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Pijpers and Ruigrok, 2006; Sugihara and Quy, 2007a; Reeber and Sillitoe, 2011; Reeber et al., 2013), the basket cell-to-Purkinje cell topography is not perfect at the zonal boundaries (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 6D and compared to cited literature.

claim: Quantification of the basket cell pinceaux using GFP fluorescence genetic marking confirms that the patterning of the pinceaux into zones reflects a significant difference in their sizes between zones.
source: Still, quantification of the basket cell pinceaux using GFP fluorescence genetic marking confirms that as a population, the patterning of the pinceaux into zones reflects a significant difference in their sizes between zones (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The genetic marking strategy labeled collateral fibers in the GL that are also restricted to Purkinje cell zones.
source: Interestingly, the genetic marking strategy labeled collateral fibers in the GL that are also restricted to Purkinje cell zones (see GL in Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation from the study shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The collaterals are prominent below the PLCβ4-expressing zones with little to no labeling in PLCβ4-negative zones.
source: The collaterals are prominent below the PLCβ4-expressing zones with little to no labeling in PLCβ4-negative zones.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: The establishment of Purkinje cell zones is dependent on a sequential series of mechanisms involving their birth date.
source: The establishment of Purkinje cell zones is dependent on a sequential (but overlapping) series of mechanisms involving their birth date (Hashimoto and Mikoshiba, 2003; Namba et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to developmental studies.

claim: The establishment of Purkinje cell zones is dependent on molecular identity.
source: molecular identity (Croci et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The establishment of Purkinje cell zones is dependent on patterning.
source: patterning (Baader et al., 1999; Sillitoe et al., 2008a)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The establishment of Purkinje cell zones is dependent on cell migration.
source: and cell migration (Larouche et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The patterning of afferents is dependent on Purkinje cell molecular processes.
source: The patterning of afferents is also dependent on these Purkinje cell molecular processes (Sillitoe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The targeting of basket axons to the AIS depends on Semaphorin 3A (Sema3A) and its receptor, neuropilin-1 (NRP1).
source: The targeting of basket axons to the AIS depends on Semaphorin 3A (Sema3A) and its receptor, neuropilin-1 (NRP1; Telley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Telley et al., 2016.

claim: Sema3A is secreted by Purkinje cells, which attracts the basket cell axons that express NRP1 toward the initial segment.
source: Sema3A is secreted by Purkinje cells, which attracts the basket cell axons that express NRP1 toward the initial segment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about molecular mechanisms of targeting.

claim: NRP1 mediates sub-cellular cell-to-cell recognition through a trans-synaptic interaction with neurofascin 186 (NF186).
source: NRP1 also mediates sub-cellular cell-to-cell recognition through a trans-synaptic interaction with neurofascin 186 (NF186), a cell adhesion molecule of the L1 immunoglobulin family that is required for the formation and maintenance of the pinceau (Ango et al., 2004; Zonta et al., 2011; Buttermore et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to molecular studies.

claim: Basket cells are born during embryogenesis.
source: However, even though basket cells are born during embryogenesis (see Figure 6E)
evidence: This is established knowledge illustrated in Figure 6E.

claim: Functional basket cell connections are formed postnatally.
source: functional basket cell connections are formed postnatally (Sotelo, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sotelo, 2008.

claim: Neuronal activity starts to remodel the cerebellar wiring diagram for function during the postnatal period.
source: a period when neuronal activity starts to remodel the cerebellar wiring diagram for function (Kano and Watanabe, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kano and Watanabe, 2019.

claim: Molecular genetics and morphogenetic programs act cooperatively with neurotransmission to shape afferent patterning.
source: Indeed, the molecular genetics and morphogenetic programs act cooperatively with neurotransmission to shape afferent patterning (Tolbert et al., 1994)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tolbert et al., 1994.

claim: Purkinje cells guide afferents into precise zones.
source: and Purkinje cells specifically guide them into precise zones (White et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2014.

claim: GABAergic neurotransmission is selectively silenced in Purkinje cells of Pcp2Cre;Slc32a1flox/flox mice.
source: We therefore tested whether Purkinje cell neurotransmission also instructs the zonal patterning of basket cell pinceaux. GABAergic neurotransmission is selectively silenced in Purkinje cells of Pcp2Cre;Slc32a1flox/flox mice (White et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2014.

claim: The Pcp2Cre allele expresses Cre during embryogenesis and continues into adulthood.
source: This particular Pcp2Cre allele is ideal for our purpose because it expresses Cre during embryogenesis and continues into adulthood (Lewis et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2004.

claim: In Pcp2Cre;Slc32a1flox/flox mutants, Purkinje cells are capable of receiving signals and firing simple spikes and complex spikes, although they cannot communicate their computations downstream via fast neurotransmission using GABA.
source: In these mutants, Purkinje cells are capable of receiving signals and firing simple spikes and complex spikes, although they cannot communicate their computations downstream via fast neurotransmission using GABA (White et al., 2014; Stay et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to White et al., 2014 and Stay et al., 2019.

claim: The mutants that lack Slc32a1 in Purkinje cells do not have a clear distinction of Purkinje cell zones or HCN1 zones, as defined by the basket cell pinceaux.
source: Compared to control Slc32a1flox/flox mice (Cre-negative, no Slc32a1 deletion; Figure 7A,C,E), the mutants that lack Slc32a1 in Purkinje cells do not have a clear distinction of Purkinje cell zones or HCN1 zones, as defined by the basket cell pinceaux (Figure 7B,D,F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 7.

claim: A uniform distribution of HCN1 was observed in the mutants, suggesting that basket cell pinceaux are all approximately the same size in the mutants.
source: Instead, we observed a uniform distribution of HCN1, suggesting that basket cell pinceaux are all approximately the same size in the mutants.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Quantification of pinceau size based on HCN1 expression confirmed that Purkinje cell neurotransmission is required for basket cell size diversity.
source: Quantification of pinceau size based on HCN1 expression confirmed that Purkinje cell neurotransmission is required for basket cell size diversity, and is the basis of their zonal plan (Figure 7G–H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding shown in Figure 7G-H.

claim: Without Purkinje cell neurotransmission, all basket cell pinceaux were not significantly different in size compared to control pinceaux within zebrinII-positive zones.
source: Without Purkinje cell neurotransmission, all basket cell pinceaux were not significantly different in size compared to control pinceaux within zebrinII-positive zones (Figure 7G–H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding shown in Figure 7G-H.

claim: Purkinje cell inhibitory neurotransmission influences basket cell diversity by sculpting pinceau structure and designating them into large versus small subsets.
source: Based on these data, we argue that Purkinje cell inhibitory neurotransmission influences basket cell diversity by sculpting pinceau structure and designating them into large versus small subsets.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The zonal plan of Purkinje cells was indistinguishable between controls and mutants when basket cell neurotransmission was silenced.
source: We then stained Purkinje cells for zebrinII and revealed that the zonal plan (Figure 8A) was indistinguishable when compared to the patterns of zones in different lobules from the anterior, central, posterior, and nodular domains (Figure 8B) between controls (Figure 8C; CreER is not expressed because the mice do not have the allele, and as a result Slc32a1 is left intact, although like the mutants, the control mice are also given tamoxifen) and mutants (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 8.

claim: Patterning of basket cell pinceaux was unaffected by the lack of basket cell neurotransmission.
source: We found that patterning of basket cell pinceaux was unaffected by this lack of basket cell neurotransmission (Figure 8K).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 8K.

claim: Inhibitory basket cell output does not control the anterior-posterior or medial-lateral patterning of molecular markers in the Purkinje cells.
source: Therefore, inhibitory basket cell output does not control the anterior-posterior or medial-lateral patterning of molecular markers in the Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: Inhibitory basket cell neurotransmission does not control the general features of zonal patterning of the basket cell pinceaux.
source: Nor does inhibitory basket cell neurotransmission control the general features of zonal patterning of the basket cell pinceaux.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: Purkinje cell neurotransmission contains the necessary instructions to restrict basket cells into a highly patterned zonal map.
source: These data also confirm that Purkinje cell neurotransmission contains the necessary instructions to restrict basket cells into a highly patterned zonal map, with a key anatomical substrate of connectivity established by segregating pinceaux into distinct sizes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: HCN1, Kv1.1, and PSD95 are all activity dependent.
source: However, we note that HCN1, Kv1.1, and PSD95 are all activity dependent (Arimitsu et al., 2009; Grosse et al., 2000; Lu et al., 2004; Subramanian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing activity-dependent regulation.

claim: 3–7 basket cells typically converge onto each Purkinje cell in control mice.
source: In control mice, 3–7 basket cells typically converge onto each Purkinje cell (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The directional growth of basket cell projections from the soma to the AIS requires an ankyrinG-dependent sub-cellular gradient of NF186.
source: The directional growth of basket cell projections from the soma to the AIS requires an ankyrinG-dependent sub-cellular gradient of NF186 (Ango et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ango et al., 2004.

claim: NF186 is expressed on Purkinje cells and trans-synaptically interacts with neuropilin-1 (NRP1) to control the formation of pinceau synapses.
source: NF186 is expressed on Purkinje cells and trans-synaptically interacts with neuropilin-1 (NRP1), a Semaphorin receptor expressed by basket cells, to control the formation of pinceau synapses (Telley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Telley et al., 2016.

claim: Basket cell GABAergic function contributes to postnatal climbing fiber synapse elimination.
source: and although basket cell GABAergic function contributes to postnatal climbing fiber synapse elimination (Nakayama et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nakayama et al., 2012.

claim: Basket cell neurotransmission does not play a role in patterning Purkinje cell zones.
source: basket cell neurotransmission does not play a role in patterning Purkinje cell zones (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: ZebrinII-positive Purkinje cells have lower firing frequencies and fire more regularly.
source: ZebrinII-positive Purkinje cells were reported to have lower firing frequencies and fire more regularly, whereas zebrinII-negative Purkinje cells have a higher firing frequency and a more irregular pattern of activity (Zhou et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiology studies.

claim: ZebrinII-negative Purkinje cells have a higher firing frequency and a more irregular pattern of activity.
source: whereas zebrinII-negative Purkinje cells have a higher firing frequency and a more irregular pattern of activity (Zhou et al., 2014; Xiao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiology studies.

claim: In vivo electrophysiology recordings demonstrate zone-specific interactions in simple spike and complex spike activity.
source: Moreover, consistent with the highly organized convergence of mossy fibers and climbing fibers within dedicated zones (Voogd et al., 2003), in vivo electrophysiology recordings demonstrate zone-specific interactions in simple spike and complex spike activity (Tang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electrophysiology studies.

claim: Purkinje cell neurotransmission is required for precisely shaping the zones into fine-grained compartments during development.
source: Interestingly, during development there is a converse relationship such that Purkinje cell neurotransmission itself is required for precisely shaping the zones into fine-grained compartments (White et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2014.

claim: ZebrinII-positive zones are predicted to have a major role in behaviors such as the vestibulo-ocular reflex, which is heavily dependent upon LTP.
source: ZebrinII-positive zones are predicted to have a major role in behaviors such as the vestibulo-ocular reflex, which is heavily dependent upon LTP, whereas behaviors such as eye-blink conditioning may be more dependent on LTD.
evidence: This is a prediction based on cited literature about synaptic plasticity.

claim: At least some portion of the eye-blink conditioning circuit is restricted to zebrinII-negative zones.
source: We know that at least some portion of the eye-blink conditioning circuit is restricted to zebrinII-negative zones (Attwell et al., 1999; Attwell et al., 2001; Mostofi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of basket cells in the deep paravermis of mouse lobule V/VI strongly modulated the timing of the blink.
source: Interestingly, optogenetic stimulation of basket cells in the deep paravermis of mouse lobule V/VI, a predominantly zebrinII-negative domain, strongly modulated the timing of the blink (Heiney et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Heiney et al., 2014.

claim: Selective elimination of basket cell output results in an increase in Purkinje cell simple spike frequency.
source: In addition, though, selective elimination of basket cell output results in an increase in Purkinje cell simple spike frequency (Brown et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown et al., 2019.

claim: Loss of Slc32a1 in Purkinje cells obscures the zonal pattern and alters learning on rotarod assays.
source: Loss of Slc32a1 in Purkinje cells obscures the zonal pattern, and therefore alters learning on rotarod assays (White et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2014.

claim: The rate and pattern of Purkinje cell neurotransmission reaches maturity around the fourth postnatal week in control mice.
source: In control mice, the rate and pattern of Purkinje cell neurotransmission reaches maturity around the fourth postnatal week (Arancillo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arancillo et al., 2015.

claim: Climbing fiber synapse strengthening and parallel fiber synapse elimination continue until ~P30.
source: For example, climbing fiber synapse strengthening and parallel fiber synapse elimination continue until ~P30 (Kano et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kano et al., 2018.

claim: Purkinje cell dendritic remodeling continues into the third postnatal week.
source: Purkinje cell dendritic remodeling continues into the third postnatal week (Kaneko et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kaneko et al., 2011.

claim: ZebrinII map refinement continues until ~P25.
source: and zebrinII map refinement continues until ~P25 (Tano et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tano et al., 1992.

claim: Purkinje cell degeneration begins at about P15 in the Purkinje cell degeneration (pcd) mutant mouse.
source: For example, Purkinje cell degeneration begins at about P15 in the Purkinje cell degeneration (pcd) mutant mouse (Landis and Mullen, 1978; reviewed in Wang and Morgan, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of the pcd mutant.

claim: Purkinje cell degeneration begins at around P8 in the Lurcher mouse.
source: and at around P8 in the Lurcher mouse (Caddy and Biscoe, 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citation to studies of the Lurcher mutant.

claim: Both pcd and Lurcher mutants lose more than 90% of their Purkinje cells before P30.
source: Both mutants lose more than 90% of their Purkinje cells before P30
evidence: This is established knowledge about these mutants.

claim: Abnormally reduced pinceau size has been noted in both pcd and Lurcher mutant mice.
source: Abnormally reduced pinceau size has been noted in both of these mutant mice (Sotelo and Alvarado-Mallart, 1987; Dumesnil-Bousez and Sotelo, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies of these mutants.

claim: Pinceau size is only modestly rescued in pcd and Lurcher animals by the introduction of grafted Purkinje cells.
source: Additionally, pinceau size is only modestly rescued in these animals by the introduction of grafted Purkinje cells (Sotelo and Alvarado-Mallart, 1987; Dumesnil-Bousez and Sotelo, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transplantation studies.

claim: Grafted Purkinje cells have normal bioelectrical properties.
source: This is despite normal bioelectrical properties (Gardette et al., 1988)
evidence: This is supported by citation to electrophysiology studies of grafted cells.

claim: Grafted Purkinje cells have zebrin-expressing compartments.
source: and the presence of zebrin-expressing compartments within grafted Purkinje cells (Rouse and Sotelo, 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citation to studies of grafted cells.

claim: 'Empty baskets' with seemingly normal pinceaux sizes remain in cases where the majority of Purkinje cell loss occurs after the differentiation and maturation of neurotransmission.
source: In contrast, in cases where the majority of Purkinje cell loss occurs after the differentiation and maturation of neurotransmission or a larger proportion of Purkinje cells remain intact in the circuit, 'empty baskets' with seemingly normal pinceaux sizes remain (Sotelo and Triller, 1979; Smeets et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: 'Prominent' baskets with 'complex' morphology have been observed in spinocerebellar ataxia type 6, SCA6.
source: For example, 'prominent' baskets with 'complex' morphology have been observed in spinocerebellar ataxia type 6, SCA6 (Lee et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2019.

claim: 'Hairy baskets' have been observed in post-mortem tissue from individuals with essential tremor.
source: and 'hairy baskets' have been observed in post-mortem tissue from individuals with essential tremor (Erickson-Davis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Erickson-Davis et al., 2010.

claim: The electrical and chemical connectivity of the ML interneurons are highly structured, with connectivity clustering coefficients that reflect a spatial arrangement in sagittal rows.
source: Regardless of their normal functions or potential pathophysiological contributions, the electrical and chemical connectivity of the ML interneurons are highly structured, with connectivity clustering coefficients that reflect a spatial arrangement in sagittal rows (Rieubland et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rieubland et al., 2014.

claim: Electrical connections tether rodent basket cells into groups of 5.
source: Electrical connections tether rodent basket cells into groups of 5 (Alcami and Marty, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alcami and Marty, 2013.

claim: Glutamate spillover from climbing fibers impacts ML interneuron function.
source: However, since basket cells contribute to the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance, and since glutamate spillover from climbing fibers impacts ML interneuron function (Szapiro and Barbour, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Szapiro and Barbour, 2007.

claim: Basket cell projections are topographically organized.
source: Our data demonstrate that basket cell projections are topographically organized
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the study's data.

claim: Basket cell patterning is dependent on proper neurotransmission in the cerebellar cortex.
source: and that their patterning is dependent on proper neurotransmission in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a main conclusion from the study's data.

claim: Basic neuroanatomical connectivity provides the underlying guiding principle for organizing the brain.
source: This study uncovers a fundamental zonal architecture of cerebellar interneuron projections and illustrates that basic neuroanatomical connectivity provides the underlying guiding principle for organizing the brain.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion drawn from the study's findings.
